\chapter{Introduction}
\newcommand{\TE}{\ensuremath{\Delta}}
The earnings losses from job displacement are large and persistent.
We estimate that the average effect \TE{} on annual earnings
is negative for up to a decade after the layoff.
The long-run \TE{} is driven by spells of non-employment
rather than by lower wage rates,
and the dispersion of \TE{} across workers is substantial.

\chapter{Model}
\newcommand{\urate}{\ensuremath{u}}
The model links displacement losses to local labour market slack.
When the aggregate rate \urate{} is high,
displaced workers queue longer,
and the effect \TE{} on earnings is amplified.
We allow \urate{} to vary at the commuting-zone level.

\chapter{Estimation}
\newcommand{\TEs}[1]{\ensuremath{\Delta_{#1}}}
Our baseline estimate \TEs{ols} compares displaced workers
to a matched control group.
The instrumented estimate \TEs{iv} exploits the timing
of closings within multi-plant firms.
Because \TEs{iv} is identified from plausibly exogenous
separations, we treat it as the headline result,
while \TE{} summarises the average loss across specifications.
Local slack enters through \urate{} measured in the year of displacement.

\chapter{Robustness}
\newcommand{\urates}[1]{\ensuremath{u_{#1}}}
Results are unchanged when slack is measured by the
sectoral rate \urates{sec} instead of the local rate.
Dropping the 2008--2009 recession years leaves \TEs{iv}
essentially unchanged,
and the aggregate \TE{} remains negative and significant.
Using \urates{nat} or \urates{cz} as alternative controls
produces nearly identical profiles,
so the headline estimates do not hinge on the slack measure,
nor on whether \urate{} enters linearly.

\chapter{Introduction}
The earnings losses from job displacement are large and persistent.
We estimate that the average effect \TE{avg} on annual earnings
is negative for up to a decade after the layoff.
The long-run \TE{avg} is driven by spells of non-employment
rather than by lower wage rates,
and the dispersion of \TE{avg} across workers is substantial.

\chapter{Model}
The model links displacement losses to local labour market slack.
When the aggregate rate \ur{nat} is high,
displaced workers queue longer,
and the effect \TE{avg} on earnings is amplified.
We allow \ur{nat} to vary at the commuting-zone level.

\chapter{Estimation}
Our baseline estimate \TE{ols} compares displaced workers
to a matched control group.
The instrumented estimate \TE{iv} exploits the timing
of closings within multi-plant firms.
Because \TE{iv} is identified from plausibly exogenous
separations, we treat it as the headline result,
while \TE{avg} summarises the average loss across specifications.
Local slack enters through \ur{nat} measured in the year of displacement.

\chapter{Robustness}
Results are unchanged when slack is measured by the
sectoral rate \ur{sec} instead of the local rate.
Dropping the 2008--2009 recession years leaves \TE{iv}
essentially unchanged,
and the aggregate \TE{avg} remains negative and significant.
Using \ur{nat} or \ur{cz} as alternative controls
produces nearly identical profiles,
so the headline estimates do not hinge on the slack measure,
nor on whether \ur{nat} enters linearly.
